name: JFrog Artifactory
license: Proprietary (a free Artifactory OSS edition covers Java artifacts)
summary: The commercial universal repository manager: one server, or JFrog’s SaaS, that hosts, proxies and promotes artifacts for more than 60 package types, from Maven and npm to Docker images and Hugging Face models.
intro: Artifactory stores the binaries a company builds and the ones it downloads, and package managers and Docker talk to it in their own protocols. JFrog lists more than 60 artifact types, including Maven, npm, PyPI, Docker, Helm, NuGet, Debian, RPM and Terraform, and it now also proxies Hugging Face and NVIDIA NGC models and stores in-house models. It runs as JFrog’s SaaS on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud regions, or self-managed, including high-availability clusters.

Repositories come in four kinds. Local repositories hold what your organization uploads. Remote repositories are caching proxies: artifacts are “only fetched (pulled) and stored (cached) on demand”, and changing metadata such as `maven-metadata.xml` or a Docker manifest is rechecked after the metadata retrieval cache period, two hours by default for most types and six for Docker, OCI and Helm OCI. Virtual repositories aggregate any number of local and remote ones behind one URL and always search local repositories first, then remote caches, then the remote repositories themselves. Federated repositories keep their contents in sync with matching repositories at other sites.

Storage is by checksum: each binary is renamed to its checksum and stored once, while the database maps checksums to repository paths, so copying, moving and promoting are database operations and identical files take no extra space. Around Artifactory, JFrog sells Xray for scanning and software composition analysis, Curation for blocking packages before they enter, and Release Lifecycle Management, where a signed release bundle is promoted from one environment to the next with `jf release-bundle-promote`.
strengths: Covers almost every ecosystem a large company uses in one product with one permission model, including system packages and AI models
Its local, remote and virtual repository model, with deterministic resolution order, became the pattern most other registries copy
Checksum-based storage deduplicates binaries and makes promotion between repositories cheap
Available as SaaS on all three big clouds or self-managed with high availability and multi-site federation
limits: Proprietary and priced per edition; the free OSS edition is aimed at Java artifacts, and scanning, curation and release bundles are separate paid products
A large system to run yourself, and a high-value target: in September 2026 CISA listed an Artifactory vulnerability (CVE-2026-82329) as exploited in the wild
Remote repositories can serve stale metadata until the cache period expires, so a just-published upstream version may not be visible at once
Backups re-expand deduplicated files into every path that references them, so they can be much larger than the filestore

snippet.title: Promote a signed release bundle to production with the JFrog CLI
source: # A release bundle groups the artifacts of a build; promoting it
# copies them into the target environment's repositories

story: In 2006 Yoav Landman was a consultant who had moved “a couple of large client projects from Ant to Maven 2” and was “frustrated by the absence of good options to manage dependencies and hosting artifacts in house”. A Codehaus outage that cut clients off from artifacts they depended on for days was “the final straw”, and he started Artifactory as an open-source project. “The quick adoption of Artifactory lead me to create JFrog around it,” he said; JFrog dates its start to 2008.

JFrog grew from Maven repositories into a platform for every package type, and ran public repositories itself: Bintray, JCenter, GoCenter and ChartCenter. It shut Bintray down on May 1, 2021, saying many of its services were now served by the JFrog Platform; GoCenter, kept read-only for years, finally shut down on February 2, 2026. JFrog went public on the Nasdaq as FROG on September 16, 2020, at $44 a share, describing itself as “the liquid software company”.

Since then Artifactory has added federated repositories for multi-site setups and Release Lifecycle Management with signed release bundles (from Artifactory 7.63.2), and has extended its formats to machine-learning models and agent packages.

choices.why: Landman’s trigger was a public repository outage. Caching each artifact the first time a build asks for it keeps builds working when upstream fails, without mirroring the whole of Maven Central.

choices.choice: Virtual repositories with a fixed order
choices.why: Build tools configured with several repositories resolve unpredictably. One URL that searches local, then cached, then remote repositories gives every build the same answer.
Artifacts are copied and moved between repositories on every promotion. Keeping one file per checksum and treating copies as database rows saves space and makes those operations fast.
